title: Predicting a Serial Criminal's Next Crime Location Using Geographical Profiling

source.pdf_page_offset_note: Physical page 1 is a one-page Summary, pages 2-3 are a two-page Executive Summary, page 4 begins the formal paper, and physical pages 5-28 correspond to printed pages 2-25.

notes: All 28 pages were read in order and every layout was visually covered.
Hit-score, focal-point, temporal, opinion-pool, pairwise-distance, decay-calibration, table, map, and reference-label details were reconciled from byte-bounded proxies or layout-aware extraction.

context_sources.summary: Geographic-profiling literature supplies residence models, spatial behavior evidence, and criticisms of proprietary or empirical constants.
Police reports, news, and SpotCrime provide nine heterogeneous event sequences.
Twenty references cover spatial behavior, mathematical profiling, expert aggregation, case evidence, and mapping.

inputs: ordered locations and times of earlier crimes linked to one offender
selected spatial or spatiotemporal model family
outputs: hit score and offender-specific rolling accuracy
decisions: where to concentrate limited investigative resources
whether historical behavior supports use for a particular offender
whether to combine the model with traditional investigation

section_map.summary: The standalone Summary compresses the decision target, behavioral premise, spatial and spatiotemporal model families, rolling hit-score metric, aggregation result, offender heterogeneity, and operational boundary into one result-first page.

The two-page Executive Summary translates the model suite into law-enforcement use conditions, names required evidence and resources, lists omitted geographic and offender features, and recommends complementing rather than replacing traditional investigation.
The formal title and Abstract repeat the target-method-metric-result-boundary chain while naming geographical profiling as the organizing mechanism.
The introduction moves from the investigative information gap to a large search-area problem, introduces geographical profiling as resource prioritization, and previews every later section.

The background defines serial crime, spatiotemporal data, spatial behavior, profiling methods, and prioritized search areas; it contrasts residence prediction with next-crime prediction and positions the paper against contested literature.

The data section admits the absence of a standardized corpus, documents police/news and SpotCrime provenance, and inventories nine heterogeneous sequences totaling 124 crimes with offender-specific temporal-decay accuracy.

The construction section states data accuracy, single-offender linkage, nonrandom rational behavior, ordered coordinates and times, a gridded search domain, sector-constant scores, and Euclidean distance.

The metric section interprets hit score as prioritized area searched before the held-out event, defines offender-level rolling accuracy, and fixes a data-dependent search square to prevent arbitrary denominator inflation.
The spatial section compares random, standard-deviation, centroid, harmonic, circle-center, median, linear-decay, and exponential-decay schemes under one sector ranking interface.
The spatiotemporal section motivates recency, defines a time-weight sequence, and transfers that weight into centroid, harmonic-mean, and distance-decay models.

The individual-results section performs rolling next-event evaluation across all sequences, separates significant improvement over random from nonsignificant differences among proposed methods, and shows no monotone gain from longer histories.

The aggregation section introduces linear and logarithmic opinion pools, calibrates decay scales from mean pairwise distance, applies a two-level factorial inclusion design, and distinguishes the numerically best equal-weight pair from statistical superiority.
The case study turns a 10.6 percent hit score into a reduction from 27,818 to 2,941 square kilometers and overlays the historical events with a Bradford-centered temporal-decay risk field.

The conclusion preserves three levels: aggregate superiority over random, no significant difference among nonrandom methods, and strong offender-specific applicability variation including a worse-than-random case.
Future work calls for a standardized large corpus, richer geographic and offender feature spaces, and an explicit cost-quality comparison between proprietary software and trained human profilers.

Twenty references connect geographic profiling, serial-crime behavior, mathematical foundations, expert aggregation, case evidence, and the Google map layer; several source typos and one incomplete citation remain visible.

assumptions.summary: All recorded spatiotemporal crime data are sufficiently accurate for ranking.
Every event in a sequence was committed by the same serial offender.
The offender's behavior is nonrandom and compatible with rational-crime spatial reasoning.
Known events are ordered as coordinates x_i and times t_i with t_1 set to zero.
A sector can be assigned one constant relative probability or score.
Euclidean distance is an adequate default despite possible road, barrier, or travel-time alternatives.
A square centered at the event mean and scaled by maximum separation is an adequate search domain.
Recent crime locations contain more information about current spatial behavior than older locations.
Component fields are compatible enough to combine through linear or logarithmic opinion pooling.
Historical Sutcliffe behavior is informative about a hypothetical next event after the observed series.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: No large standardized corpus was available, so events were assembled from police/news sources and SpotCrime-linked reports.
Table 1 records nine sequences, 124 crimes, and offender-specific temporal exponential-decay accuracy scores.
Events are represented as ordered coordinates and times and the domain is discretized into constant-score sectors.
At every forecast origin the search domain is centered at the known-event mean with side twice the maximum pairwise separation.

models.summary: The ordered spatial observations interface retains spatial event domain: Represent the ordered known crime locations inside the search region.
The ordered event times interface retains time ordering: Preserve forecast-origin order and define elapsed-event chronology.
The grid score field interface retains sector constant score: Discretize the continuous search area into ranked sectors.
The square grid resolution interface retains grid count: Relate search extent and cell resolution.
The strict rank set interface retains better-ranked sector set: Collect sectors ranked strictly above the sector containing the next event.
The prioritized search fraction interface retains hit score: Measure the fraction of the search area visited before the held-out sector.
The offender-specific rolling mean interface retains criminal accuracy: Average forward hit scores after the minimum three-event history.
The data-dependent square extent interface retains search square: Fix a reproducible denominator for cross-model hit-score comparison.
The axis-aligned dispersion region interface retains standard deviation rectangle: Define a rectangular search region from coordinate dispersion.
The trend-aligned dispersion region interface retains standard deviation ellipse: Define a least-squares-oriented elliptical search region.
The inverse-distance score interface retains centralization score: Rank sectors by distance from a selected focal point.
The arithmetic focal point interface retains centroid: Estimate a single central focal point.
The harmonic focal point interface retains harmonic mean focal point: Construct the paper's harmonic-mean center.
The diameter midpoint focal point interface retains circle center: Use the midpoint of the most separated crimes as a focal point.
The multi-event additive field interface retains probability distance field: Accumulate contributions from every previous event instead of one center.
The linear distance score interface retains linear decay: Decrease the sector contribution linearly with distance.
The exponential distance score interface retains exponential decay: Decrease the sector contribution exponentially with distance.
The recency weight interface retains temporal weight: Give later events more influence while keeping the first event nonzero.
The weight normalizer interface retains total temporal weight: Normalize weighted focal-point calculations.
The weighted focal point interface retains temporal centroid: Shift the focal point toward recent events.
The weighted harmonic focal point interface retains temporal harmonic mean: Apply the paper's recency weighting to its harmonic center.
The weighted multi-event field interface retains temporal probability distance: Weight every event's distance contribution by recency.
The weighted additive ensemble interface retains linear opinion pool: Combine compatible model fields through a weighted sum.
The weighted multiplicative ensemble interface retains logarithmic opinion pool: Combine model fields through a weighted product.
The corpus scale statistic interface retains mean pairwise distance: Set a sequence-specific spatial scale for ensemble components.
The zero-at-mean-distance rule interface retains linear decay calibration: Scale the linear component before pooling.
The mean-distance exponential rule interface retains exponential decay calibration: Scale the exponential component before pooling.
Assign sector scores independently at random and use expected hit score 0.5 as the reference.
Build one- and two-standard-deviation rectangles and ellipses as coverage regions rather than fully ranked fields.
For each event from the fourth onward, fit only on its predecessors, score the held-out sector, and average the hit scores.
Run random, centralization, probability-distance, and temporal variants on all nine sequences and compare aggregate hit scores with uncertainty.
For each candidate component, compare equal-weight inclusion and exclusion across all two-level combinations for linear and logarithmic pools.
Fit temporal exponential decay to the historical series, calculate the case hit score, convert it to square kilometers, and map the highest-risk region.

dependency_graph.handoff: Ordered events and the region are discretized into sector-level scores.
The count of sectors above the held-out sector becomes the hit-score numerator.
Sequential hit scores become offender-specific historical accuracy.
The common square fixes the domain on which centralization scores are ranked.
The centroid supplies one focal point to the centralization field.
The additive field receives an exponential distance kernel.
Temporal weights shift the centroid toward recent events.
Temporal weights scale each event's distance contribution.
Mean pairwise distance supplies the pooled exponential scale.
Temporal exponential decay becomes one candidate field in the linear opinion pool.
Circle-center centralization becomes the second component of the best reported equal-weight pool.
Finite inclusion search selects the component set evaluated by the opinion pool.

verification.summary: Nine sequences and 124 crimes are inventoried with one offender-specific temporal exponential-decay score per sequence.
verification.strength: Exposes heterogeneity and case imbalance instead of reporting only an aggregate.
verification.limitation: The corpus is small, opportunistic, and not standardized.

verification.summary: Each event from the fourth onward is predicted only from earlier events and converted to a hit score.
verification.strength: Preserves temporal order and produces multiple held-out predictions per sequence.
verification.limitation: Tie handling, cell size, and parameter tuning provenance remain incomplete.

verification.summary: One common data-dependent square fixes the denominator used by all ranked models at each origin.
verification.strength: Prevents unlimited low-score padding from trivially reducing the hit score.
verification.limitation: The factor and square geometry are not sensitivity-tested.

verification.summary: All proposed models are compared with a random baseline over the complete corpus.
verification.strength: Provides one common operational metric and an explicit null reference.
verification.limitation: The significance test and inferential unit are not reported.

verification.summary: Hit score is plotted against the number of previously observed crimes with 50 percent confidence intervals.
verification.strength: Checks whether more observations visibly improve performance.
verification.limitation: The confidence level is unconventional and sample counts are hidden.

verification.summary: Table 2 reports exact mean hit scores and 95 percent confidence quantities for ten models.
verification.strength: Separates random, simple, and temporal variants under one table.
verification.limitation: The confidence column is not labeled explicitly as half-width or interval.

verification.summary: A two-level factorial inclusion design compares equal-weight model subsets for two pool types.
verification.strength: Includes component-alone and subset comparisons through a finite design.
verification.limitation: Selection and performance reporting reuse the same small corpus.

verification.summary: The best linear pool reports 0.081 plus or minus 0.027 but is not claimed statistically superior.
verification.strength: Correctly distinguishes numeric best from inferential dominance.
verification.limitation: No nested validation estimates ensemble-selection optimism.

verification.summary: The Sutcliffe case converts 10.6 percent into 2,941 of 27,818 square kilometers.
verification.strength: The physical-area ratio agrees with the reported hit score.
verification.limitation: No counterfactual investigation outcome or cost comparison is available.

verification.summary: D.C. sniper 0.056 and Columbus serial rapist 0.533 are contrasted.
verification.strength: Demonstrates that aggregate success does not guarantee case-level usefulness.
verification.limitation: No abstention threshold or pre-use diagnostic is calibrated.

results_trace.summary: Random is about 0.5 while individual nonrandom models cluster around 0.092-0.125.
Temporal exponential decay is the lowest-scoring individual model at 0.092 plus or minus 0.029.
Equal temporal exponential decay and circle center gives the best reported linear-pool mean 0.081 plus or minus 0.027.
The Sutcliffe priority region is reduced from 27,818 to 2,941 square kilometers, consistent with 10.6 percent.
Case performance ranges from 0.056 for the D.C. sniper to 0.533 for the Columbus serial rapist, worse than random.

contributions.summary: Defines an operational searched-area hit score and offender-specific rolling accuracy.
Places focal-point and multi-event distance fields under a common sector-ranking interface.
Transfers recency weights into both focal-point and distance-field models.
Uses linear and logarithmic opinion pools to combine compatible spatial fields.
Uses a factorial inclusion design and explicitly separates numerical best from statistical superiority.
Translates a dimensionless score into a physical search-area decision.

writing_logic.summary: Summary chain: target -> premise -> model families -> rolling metric -> aggregate result -> offender heterogeneity -> practical boundary.
Executive chain: intended use -> model options -> applicability checks -> omitted information -> human-model complementarity.
Introduction chain: weak traditional clues -> oversized search area -> geographical profiling -> limited-resource allocation -> roadmap.
Formalization chain: assumptions -> ordered events -> sector grid -> score field -> distance choice.
Metric chain: operational search motive -> strict rank set -> hit fraction -> rolling offender score -> fixed domain.
Model chain: random and region baselines -> focal-point methods -> multi-event fields -> recency extensions.
Aggregation chain: no clear individual winner -> opinion pools -> scale calibration -> factorial inclusion -> bounded result.
Deployment chain: case events -> model hit score -> square-kilometer reduction -> map priority -> caution.

language_observations.summary: The summary fits target, assumptions, methods, metric, result, and applicability boundary into one evidence-dense page.
Applicability conditions are framed as questions an agency can answer before use.
Limitations precede the recommendation, preventing the executive summary from sounding promotional.
The introduction converts an information-gap narrative into a resource-allocation abstraction.
Given-Let-Then definitions create a clean bridge from symbols to operational meaning.
The text distinguishes significant improvement over random from lack of significant differences among proposed methods.
Numerically best is explicitly kept separate from statistically better.
A dimensionless score is translated into square kilometers for decision-makers.
Aggregate claims are immediately bounded by a worse-than-random offender case.
Future work maps each omission to data, feature, or cost evidence rather than using generic improvement language.

visualization_observations.summary: Shows the complete task-method-metric-result-boundary chain on one competition summary sheet.
Turns model validity into linkage, historical accuracy, and resource-capacity checks.
Keeps omitted geography, omitted offender features, and human comparison visible beside the recommendation.
Confirms full route and absence of an appendix.
Audits nine sequences, 124 crimes, and the extreme offender-specific spread from 0.020 to 0.517.
Defines the square grid sectors and cell-resolution interface used by every ranking model.
Contrasts a single centroid hotspot with an exponential field concentrated around all observed crimes.
Shows how temporal weighting moves the field toward the recent end of an eastward sequence.
Compares aggregate hit scores for random and all individual models with uncertainty bars.
Shows unstable hit score by number of observed crimes with 50 percent confidence intervals.
Provides exact mean hit scores and 95 percent confidence half-widths for ten models.
Shows the pure circle-center endpoint of the opinion-pool weight sweep.
Shows intermediate hotspot movement and shape under 0.25/0.75 and 0.50/0.50 weights.
Shows the transition to a pure exponential-decay field.
Compares one-standard-deviation rectangle and ellipse search regions for Peter Sutcliffe.
Maps the Sutcliffe event locations on recognizable geography with a physical scale.
Shows the Bradford-centered temporal exponential-decay risk field and secondary Manchester hotspot.

judge_relevance_hypotheses.summary: The complete result-to-boundary Summary plausibly improves traceability for judges without proving correctness.
Explicitly refusing to equate numeric best with statistical dominance plausibly increases credibility.
Converting hit score to physical search area plausibly strengthens operational relevance.

weaknesses.summary: Hit score counts only sectors strictly above the held-out sector and does not specify tie ordering, so tied fields can receive optimistically small search fractions.
Hit score is denominator-sensitive; the twice-maximum-distance search square is reproducible but heuristic and lacks size, shape, and grid-resolution sensitivity.
The inverse-distance centralization score is singular if a sector representative coincides with the focal point.
The harmonic mean of two-dimensional coordinates is mathematically ambiguous and can be unstable at zero or across signed coordinate values.
Linear decay can become negative, so the quantity is not a probability unless truncated or explicitly treated only as a ranking score.
The claim that exponential-decay constants do not affect hit-score ranking is generally false because changing gamma can reorder sums of several exponential contributions.
Temporal normalization uses t_n rather than explicitly t_n-t_1, making the formula dependent on how the time origin is encoded.
With k=0.1 and t_1=0, the last-to-first temporal weight ratio is 11 rather than the stated approximately ten.
The fixed temporal offset k=0.1 has no calibration, uncertainty, or sensitivity analysis.
The random baseline assigns independent random sector values, but reproducibility seeds and tie behavior are not reported.
The statement that all proposed methods significantly outperform random does not name the test, p-value, multiplicity handling, or exact inferential unit.
Figure 5 uses 50 percent confidence intervals without explaining the unconventional level or displaying sample sizes by history length.
The corpus contains only nine heterogeneous sequences and 124 crimes, with large imbalance from 6 to 40 crimes per sequence.
Performance varies sharply by offender; the Columbus serial rapist score is worse than random even though aggregate performance is favorable.
Aggregation weights, inclusion choices, and decay calibration are developed and evaluated on the same small corpus, creating tuning-selection optimism.
The meaning of the Table 2 confidence column is not explicit in the header; prose implies it is a plus-or-minus half-width.
The exponential calibration gamma=sqrt(2/delta_bar) is asserted through a desired mean-distance relationship without a full derivation under the pooled field.
The cost-resource recommendation remains qualitative and does not measure software cost, investigator training cost, search capacity, or error consequences.
The paper sometimes calls lower-is-better hit score an accuracy value, which can invert the intuitive direction for readers.
Reference text contains source-level spelling errors and one incomplete citation, limiting bibliographic reproducibility.

independent_extensions.summary: Specify randomized or midrank tie treatment and report cumulative area-search curves over grid resolutions.
Tune and stress-test search-domain center, shape, scale, and cell size inside rolling origins.
Replace heuristic recency weights with calibrated decay families selected in nested rolling validation.
Normalize and calibrate component fields before pooling and estimate ensemble weights without using evaluation outcomes.
Build case-level diagnostics and an abstention rule for offenders whose historical accuracy is unstable or worse than baseline.
Evaluate map, software, staffing, and false-priority costs against trained-human and simple-baseline workflows.

candidate_rule_impacts.action: retain result-first summaries, parallel model-family prose, Given-Let-Then definitions, and numeric-versus-significant claim boundaries
retain source and sequence provenance while requiring standardized event tables, coordinates, linkage uncertainty, and versioning
retain explicit metric and distance interfaces while requiring calibration against road-time and simpler geometric baselines
distinguish relative sector scores from probabilities and require nonnegative normalized dynamic fields
retain explicit opinion-pool fusion only after target, scale, normalization, and weight compatibility checks
retain rolling-origin hit-score evaluation while adding ties, resolution, calibration, and a fuller baseline suite
make reliability offender-specific and require diagnostics plus abstention for worse-than-baseline cases
retain geography, scale bars, observed events, aligned risk fields, and physical search-area interpretation
retain resource-capacity and human-model complementarity as explicit deployment conditions
compare all spatial, temporal, and aggregate variants under one forecast origin, domain, metric, and uncertainty protocol
